mcqs.question: When extracting nouns from a parking lot requirements list, why doesn't "license plate" get its own class the way "vehicle" and "ticket" do?
options: License plate has no independent state or behavior of its own — it's a string attribute that belongs to Vehicle
Nouns are only turned into classes if they appear in the first sentence of the requirements
License plates should always be modeled as a separate class in any real-world design
Only nouns that are also verbs elsewhere in the requirements become classes
mcqs.explanation: The test isn't sentence position or grammar tricks — it's whether the noun has independent state and behavior worth tracking on its own. Vehicle and Ticket qualify; license plate is just a value they hold.

mcqs.question: You're deciding whether Car should inherit from Vehicle, and whether ParkingSpot should inherit from Vehicle. What's the right call and why?
options: Neither should inherit from Vehicle, since inheritance should never be used in LLD interviews
Car should inherit from Vehicle, since a car is a kind of vehicle; ParkingSpot should not, since a spot doesn't hold a vehicle, it's occupied by one
ParkingSpot should inherit from Vehicle because a spot and a vehicle are closely related in the domain
Both should inherit from Vehicle, since both appear in the same requirements list
mcqs.explanation: The is-a test decides it: a car genuinely is a kind of vehicle, so inheritance fits. A spot merely relates to a vehicle (holds a reference to one) — that's has-a or association, not is-a. Inheritance isn't banned, and shared appearance in requirements doesn't imply a type relationship.

mcqs.question: A candidate creates a separate class for every noun in the requirements, including "entry timestamp" and "fee amount." What's the problem?
options: There is no problem — every noun should always become its own class
The only downside is that it takes longer to draw on the whiteboard
Most of those nouns are attributes with no independent state or behavior, and turning them into classes adds indirection without adding meaning
Timestamps and amounts should instead be modeled as global variables
mcqs.explanation: Entry timestamp and fee amount have no behavior of their own — they're data that belongs to Ticket. Fragmenting them into classes doesn't just cost drawing time, it obscures which classes actually carry meaningful responsibility, which is what interviewers watch for.

mcqs.question: Your ParkingLot class has grown to 15 methods covering pricing, spot assignment, and ticketing. What does this most likely indicate?
options: The class is appropriately sized for an intermediate-level LLD problem
The class needs even more methods before it can be considered complete
The class should simply be renamed, but its structure is otherwise fine
The model is too flat and responsibilities should be split into separate classes like pricing and ticketing
mcqs.explanation: A class you can't describe in one sentence without "and" is a sign of a too-flat model — pricing, spot assignment, and ticketing are separable responsibilities. Adding more methods or just renaming the class wouldn't fix the underlying issue; splitting it would.
